subtitulo: 1453, the diaspora that fed the Renaissance, and the manufacture of an operative nostalgia

coda.heading: Close of the block and coda for the journey
intro: This is the end of the first block. Let us retrace the thread we have built over eight entries, because it is worth holding as a structure before entering the Ottoman world. First: a geography of maritime nodes that makes autarky impossible and dependence necessary (entry 1). Second: political communities of extremely high participatory intensity resting on fragile states, which destroy one another and fail to federate (entries 1 and 2). Third: absorption by an external power that respects civic forms while emptying out sovereignty (entries 3 and 4). Fourth: the conversion of one's own past into heritage administered by others, with simultaneous veneration and contempt (entry 5). Fifth: a religious and state identity that later nationalism will have to rewrite (entry 6). Sixth: an insular periphery with a Western colonial structure, distinct from the mainland (entry 7). Seventh: defeat metabolized into operative nostalgia (entry 8). The five blocks that follow are variations on these seven elements.

items.text: For the journey, three concrete observations. In Athens, the Byzantine Museum and the church of Panagia Kapnikarea, in the middle of Ermou Street, hemmed in between shops: the modern city was built around it in the nineteenth century, and its survival is owed to a personal intervention by King Ludwig I of Bavaria. An eleventh-century temple saved by a German monarch in a city that was reinventing itself as classical: the whole entry in a single commercial corner.

In Corfu, return to Saint Spyridon with what you now know. The relic arrived in 1456, three years after the fall, brought by refugees from Constantinople via Epirus. The island's patron saint is, literally, a 1453 exile. Corfiot identity is organized around an object that arrived in flight. Ask whether people know that origin, and you will see how memory works: rites are preserved far more faithfully than reasons.

And a question to bring to any taverna table: what is the fall of the City to the person you're speaking with — just "the City," I POLI, without a name, because in Greek Constantinople needs no name. Listen for whether the sleeping emperor comes up. And think, meanwhile, of the head growing underground in Puquio.

sections.heading: What actually fell on May 29, 1453
paragraphs: The siege lasted fifty-three days, from April 6 to May 29, 1453. Mehmed II was twenty-one years old and commanded an army that modern estimates put between fifty and eighty thousand men, plus the artillery of the Hungarian engineer Urban, who had first offered his services to the Byzantine emperor: the emperor could not afford them. The defenders numbered about seven thousand, of whom close to two thousand were foreigners, mostly Genoese and Venetian. The chain closing off the Golden Horn was circumvented by hauling ships overland on greased rollers. Constantine XI Palaiologos died fighting on the wall, and his body was never identified with certainty.

Now the nuance the epic conceals. The city that fell had perhaps fifty thousand inhabitants within walls built for half a million; there were neighborhoods turned into orchards and fields inside the enclosure. The empire had shrunk to practically the city itself and a fragment of the Peloponnese. It had been paying tribute for a century. In 1439, at the Council of Florence, it had accepted union with Rome in exchange for military aid that never arrived, and that acceptance split its own population: the phrase attributed to Admiral Loukas Notaras — "better to see the Turkish turban reigning in the city than the Latin miter" — sums up a majority position among the lower clergy and the common people. In other words: a considerable share of the defenders preferred Ottoman conquest to religious submission to the West.

The analytical conclusion is uncomfortable and necessary: 1453 WAS NOT A RUPTURE, IT WAS A NOTARIZATION. It legally certified a fact that had already been settled for decades. Catastrophic dates usually work this way, and their function is narrative: they allow what was a process of centuries to be pinned to a single day, and therefore allow one to imagine that without that day everything would have been different. 1532 performs the same service in the Peruvian narrative. Cajamarca does not explain the fall of Tahuantinsuyo; the civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa, the smallpox epidemic that preceded the Spaniards and killed Huayna Cápac, and the alliances of subjugated peoples with the invaders explain far more. But a date with a protagonist is more manageable than a process with multiple causes.

sections.heading: The diaspora that made the Renaissance (and its price)
paragraphs: Decades before and after the fall, Greek scholars emigrated to Italy carrying manuscripts and the capacity to read them. Manuel Chrysoloras taught Greek in Florence from 1397. George Gemistos Plethon, at the Council of Ferrara-Florence in 1438–1439, expounded Plato before an Italian audience that knew Aristotle only through Latin translations from the Arabic, and impressed Cosimo de' Medici enough that he founded the Platonic Academy. Cardinal Bessarion, a Greek convert to Catholicism, assembled a library of more than seven hundred manuscripts that he bequeathed to Venice and that forms the core of the Marciana. And from 1495 onward, Aldus Manutius's press in Venice began publishing the Greek classics with typefaces designed for the purpose, employing exiled Greek proofreaders and correctors.

Traditional historiography presents this as the Greek gift to Europe. It is more precise to say something else: Greek culture survived by becoming the INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY OF THE WEST. The texts were saved; the collective subject that had produced and transmitted them remained under Ottoman rule for four centuries, and when it reappeared as a nation in the nineteenth century, it found its own tradition handed back to it edited, translated, canonized, and explained by German, French, and English philologists, who moreover held opinions on whether modern Greeks were worthy heirs. The operation is structurally identical to that of the Parthenon marbles, and to that of the Andean manuscripts, ceramics, and textiles preserved and studied in museums of the North. The preservation is real and valuable; so is the asymmetry.

It is also worth not idealizing the flight. Most Greeks did not emigrate: they stayed put, and their history under the Ottoman Empire — four centuries — is the subject of the block that begins in the next entry. The story of the enlightened diaspora, appealing because it connects to the Renaissance and to the West, has for a long time functioned as an elegant way of not looking at what happened to the vast majority who remained.

sections.heading: Two sleeping kings: marble and Inkarrí
paragraphs: Here we arrive at the comparative core of this entry, and it is among the findings that justify the mirror exercise all by itself.

Greek popular tradition elaborated, after 1453, the myth of the MARBLE EMPEROR, the Marmaroménos Vasiliás: Constantine XI did not die; an angel snatched him away at the last instant and turned him to marble, and he sleeps in a cave beneath the Golden Gate until the day an angel wakes him, returns his sword to him, and returns him to Constantinople to reconquer it. One variant tells that the priest who was celebrating the liturgy in Hagia Sophia when the Turks entered walked into the wall with the chalice, and that he will emerge to finish the mass exactly where he left off, when the city becomes Christian again. A popular song repeated: "once again, with the years, with time, once again they will be ours."

Andean popular tradition elaborated, after the execution of Atahualpa in 1533 and above all after the dismemberment of Túpac Amaru II in 1781, the myth of INKARRÍ: the Inca's head, buried, is growing underground and slowly reconstituting its body; when the body is complete, the Inca will return and the world will turn over — the PACHACUTI — and the just order will be restored. Arguedas collected versions in Puquio in the 1950s; Flores Galindo built his analysis of the Andean utopia as a long-term political matrix on that material.

The two myths share a remarkable formal structure: a sovereign not dead but suspended, an incomplete or petrified body, an underground space, and a return that will reverse the defeat. No historical contact between the two traditions is possible; what exists is a convergent response to the same problem. When a society suffers a total defeat it can neither process nor reverse, it produces a device that keeps open the possibility of reversal without demanding immediate action. It is simultaneously consolation and reserve: it postpones revenge while keeping it available.

And both myths were activated politically once conditions changed. The sleeping emperor fed the MEGALI IDEA, the irredentist project of reconquering Constantinople and the Greek lands of Anatolia, which structured Greek foreign policy from 1844 to the disaster of 1922 — we will see it in Block IV — and which cost hundreds of thousands of lives and the uprooting of a million and a half people. Inkarrí fed the rebellion of Túpac Amaru II in 1780–1781 and reappeared, resemanticized, in the millenarian discourses of twentieth-century Peru. Nostalgia is not an innocuous sentiment: it is a STORED POLITICAL RESOURCE, and when activated it determines wars and programs. This is probably the single most important observation you can carry with you for reading everything that follows, in Greece and in Peru.

sections.heading: What Mehmed did the next day
paragraphs: The conqueror's policy deserves attention because it prefigures the entire next block. Mehmed II did not exterminate or expel the Orthodox population: he organized it. In 1454 he appointed Gennadios Scholarios patriarch — precisely the leader of the anti-unionist party, that is, the man who had opposed union with Rome. He granted him civil authority over all the Orthodox Christians of the empire: jurisdiction over marriage, inheritance, education, and the collection of certain taxes. Thus was born the MILLET system, the indirect government by religious community that would structure four centuries.

The calculation is transparent and effective: by empowering the anti-Western faction of the Church, Mehmed ensured that the principal institution of his new subjects had a vested interest in the permanence of Ottoman rule and in the rupture with Rome. The Orthodox Church obtained under the sultan an administrative power over its flock that it had never held under the Christian emperor. It is a textbook example of how a conquering power co-opts the intermediary elite of the conquered, and it has its exact equivalent in Spanish policy toward the Andean curacas, who kept privileges, taxation rights, and local authority in exchange for functioning as a gear in the colonial machine. In both cases the long-term consequence is the same: when nationalism arrives, the institution that preserved identity will also be the one that collaborated with domination, and that ambivalence will prove impossible to resolve cleanly.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world: 1453, 1492, 1532
paragraphs: The year 1453 is a global crossroads. The Hundred Years' War also ends. Gutenberg prints around 1450–1455. Portugal advances along the African coast. In 1492 Granada will fall, the Jews will be expelled from Spain — many of whom will be welcomed by the Ottoman sultan and will found the Sephardic community of Salonika, which will remain a majority in that city until the twentieth century — and Columbus will cross the Atlantic. In 1498 Vasco da Gama will reach India by sea, permanently displacing the trade routes of the eastern Mediterranean and condemning Venice to a long decline.

And in 1532 Tahuantinsuyo will fall. Eighty years separate the fall of Constantinople from that of Cajamarca. The two episodes share more than the distance suggests: a centralized empire beheaded at its apex; a local elite negotiating its survival with the conqueror; a state religion imposed over the temples of the defeated; a new administrative language superimposed on one's own; and a popular memory that produces a sleeping king. They also share a decisive difference that should not be erased: the Ottomans did not bring new diseases or demographically destroy the conquered population, whereas the American conquest produced a demographic collapse of unprecedented proportions, with estimates placing the fall of the Andean population at more than two-thirds within the first century. The mirror serves to think, not to equate.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: Hagia Sophia and nostalgia as foreign policy
paragraphs: The contemporary activation of 1453 is continuous and verifiable. In July 2020, Turkey reversed Hagia Sophia's museum status — in effect since 1934 — and reconverted it into a mosque. In May 2024 it did the same with the church of the Holy Savior in Chora and its fourteenth-century mosaics. Both decisions provoked formal protests from Greece, from UNESCO, and from the Orthodox churches, and both should be read for what they are: internal gestures of identity mobilization with calculated external effects. The conquest of 1453 is commemorated every May 29 in Turkey with official ceremonies.

On the Greek side, nostalgia operates in a more diffuse but equally real way: in the liturgy, in school instruction, in the naming of the Patriarchate of Constantinople — never "of Istanbul" —, and in the symbolic weight of a city that was Greek and today harbors barely a few thousand Greeks, after the effective expulsion of the community through the pogrom of September 1955 and the expulsions of 1964, episodes that official Turkish historiography minimizes and that Greek historiography remembers precisely. In 2024–2026, with a real but crisis-management-limited Greek-Turkish diplomatic thaw, none of these questions of memory is on the table: they are postponed because they have no negotiated solution.

The transferable lesson is the one already stated: nostalgia is a stored resource that states administer. In Peru, the memory of the internal armed conflict of 1980–2000, the debate over the Place of Memory, the disputes over how victims and perpetrators are named, and the electoral use of terruqueo function by the same mechanics: the past is not remembered, it is mobilized. And whoever controls the vocabulary with which the past is named controls a substantial part of what can be said about the present. Thucydides, in entry 1, had already seen it at Corcyra.
